list.listitem: Malnutrition may cause impaired immune response, wound healing, muscle strength (including respiratory), thermoregulation, psychosocial functioning. B

Candidates for nutrition support include critically ill patients who will not be fed for over 1 week, C high-risk surgical patients, B or malnourished patients or patients at significant risk for malnutrition. A
Nutritional support of malnourished patients should begin with oral interventions, and if unsuccessful or unsafe, enteral or parenteral feedings may be used to meet nutritional goals. A
Enteral feeding is preferred over parenteral nutrition if the GI tract is intact and is functioning. A
No evidence supports clinical benefit of tube feeding in the demented elderly. A
Enteral nutrition is the delivery of a nutritionally complete feed via the GI tract. Parenteral nutrition is the intravenous administration of nutrients via central or peripheral catheter.
Refeeding syndrome may occur in up to 25% of cancer patients; malnutrition occurs in up to 40% in ICU patients.

Malnutrition may cause impaired immune response, wound healing, muscle strength (including respiratory), thermoregulation, psychosocial functioning. Malnutrition may increase water and electrolyte disturbances, risk for falls, inactivity (pressure ulcers, thromboembolism), vitamin/mineral deficiencies.
Infection rate is significantly higher in critically ill patients receiving parenteral nutrition as compared with enteral nutrition.
See for a summary of recommendations for nutritional support.

Malnutrition risk may be assessed using established tools, including the calculation of body mass index (BMI = kg/m2) and/or encompass factors including appetite, weight loss over time etc. (eg, Glasgow nutritional screening tool).

Especially, consider nutritional support for critically ill patients who are malnourished or who will not be fed for over 1 week, for high-risk surgical patients who are due to undergo major abdominal procedures or within 48 hours postsurgery in high-risk general surgery patients, and for malnourished patients or patients at significant risk for malnutrition with unsafe oral intake or nonfunctional GI tract.
Nutrition support teams are cost-effective and result in improved outcomes.
There is not enough evidence to support the use of nutritional supplements to prolong life or improve quality of life in palliative care patients.
There is inadequate evidence to assess the benefit of dietary advice to improve mortality in disease-related malnutrition.
There are no trials to determine if enteral tube feeding is effective compared to continuation of oral feeding in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
A meta-analysis of low-quality evidence shows nutritional support therapy for malnourished inpatients may improve readmission rates but has no effect on mortality or physical function.
There is limited evidence on the use of dietary advice with or without oral nutritional supplementation for disease related malnutrition.

Dysphagia treatment, including a speech language pathologist evaluation, oral supplementation, food fortification, altered texture diets) should be attempted, if applicable, prior to consideration of nutrition support.
In adults with swallowing disturbances, percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tubes lead to less intervention failure than nasogastric tubes, but there is no difference in complications or mortality.

Bolus feeding is as effective as continuous feeding; the decision is based upon patient preference, convenience for staff and drug administration. Bolus feeding may be useful for patients who pull out their feeding tube, critically ill patients with severe illness, patients with delayed gastric emptying, and patients who go to therapy sessions.

If residual content is high (over 200-300 mL), the pump rate may be reduced or metoclopramide can be administered to increase GI motility. If unsuccessful, postpyloric enteral tube feeding or parenteral nutrition should be considered.

Evaluate for risk of refeeding syndrome, which is a rapid fall in phosphate, magnesium, and potassium, and a shift in fluid to extracellular spaces in malnourished patients who receive carbohydrates. Limit fluid and monitor electrolytes until stabilized.
For critical care patients, nasogastric feedings are safer and more practical if delivered continuously over 24 hours, which will moderate swings in serum glucose.
In patients with acute lung injury, there is no difference between short-term low-energy permissive underfeeding ("trophic feeding") and full enteral feeds.
If pancreatic rest is required, elemental formula should be used, delivered postduodenally.

Energy dense versus usual enternal nutrition: In a randomized trial of mechanically ventilated patients (n = 3957), energy dense enteral nutrition (1.5 kcal/ml) did not improve any clinical outcomes compared with routine enteral nutrition (1.0 kcal/ml).
GI Bleeding: for patients with GI bleeding, a systematic review (5 studies, 313 patients) found no difference in rates or rebleeding or mortality between early and delayed enteral nutrition.
Parenteral nutrition should be used when oral or enteral feeding is either ineffective in maintaining nutritional status or unsafe.

Peripheral parenteral nutrition is used when nutritional support is anticipated for less than 14 days. Examples include patients with chronic intestinal failure, short bowel syndrome, malabsorption, fistula formation, and GI obstruction.

Central parenteral nutrition is used when nutritional support is anticipated for greater than 14 days. Examples include patients with neuromuscular swallowing disorder, physiological anorexia, upper GI obstruction, GI dysfunction or malabsorption, and increased nutritional requirements.
Administer 50% of estimated caloric needs for the first 24 to 48 hours and supplement with daily parenteral multivitamins and parenteral trace elements.
Continuous delivery is the preferred method for critically ill patients.

ICU patients: a systematic review (8 RCTs, 5360 patients) found no difference regarding length of stay or mortality and a small increase in respiratory infections (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.01-1.24) with combined parenteral and enteral nutrition compared with enteral nutrition alone.
See for recommendations regarding laboratory and clinical monitoring.
Glucose monitoring 1 to 2 times a day until stable, then weekly.
Diarrhea: increase fluid to meet losses, rule out other causes, and consider change of feeding formulation.
Vomiting: elevate head of bed 45 degrees 1 hour before and 1 hour after feedings. Rule out other etiologies.
Patients should have adequate energy and nutrient intake (~60% of estimated needs) before stopping nutrition support.
Low-birth-weight infants: Parenteral nutrition should not be used if oral or enteral nutrient delivery is possible.

Higher levels of enteral intake (trophic feedings and advancing feedings) require significantly less time to reach full feeding status and results in significant or near significant reduction in hospital stay.
Early enteral nutrition in critically ill children is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with delayed enteral nutrition based mainly on observational studies.
No evidence supports clinical benefit of tube feeding in the demented elderly.
Providing enteral or parenteral nutrition at the end of life or in demented patients may worsen quality of life and should be avoided unless advanced directives specify nutrition support.

section.type: Supplements to enteral and parenteral nutrition
section.heading: Supplements to enteral and parenteral nutrition

list.listitem: Modular protein may be added to enteral feedings to meet patient’s estimated needs if higher than provided by the formula.
Fish oils, borage oils, and antioxidants may decrease the risk of infectious complications but not change overall mortality rates.
High arginine content enteral feeds are not generally recommended but are associated with reduction in infectious complications.
There is insufficient evidence to support routine use of enteral glutamine in burn and trauma patients.
Parenteral nutrition glutamine is recommended for critically ill patients to improve outcomes by reducing incidence of serious sepsis.

Probiotics may be helpful in addressing GI issues such as lactose intolerance, reducing diarrhea and/or abdominal bloating; however, standard dosing recommendations do not exist. Probiotics may increase mortality in patients with pancreatitis.
Therapy referred to as immunonutrition does not decrease mortality after surgery. In high-quality studies there is no improvement in post-operative complications with immunonutrition.

cell.label: Patient malnourished or at risk for malnutrition.

Implement oral interventions: dysphagia treatment, altered consistency diet, fortification or supplementation of oral intake, assistance at mealtime, liberalization of therapeutic diet. Malnutrition or risk for malnutrition continues?
Monitor effectiveness of intervention with ongoing screening for malnutrition (weekly for inpatients).
Gastrostomy or NG tube ± oral nutrition; if impaired gastric emptying and prokinetics not successful, consider jejunal feeding. Adequate nutrient intake?
Stop or reduce nutritional support when oral intake meets ~60% of nutritional needs and maintains nutritional status.

feature.caption: Nutritional, Clinical and Laboratory Monitoring of Patients Receiving Specialized Nutritional Support (Enteral and Parenteral Nutrition).

tr.td: Initially
• Nutrient intake, fluid balance (I/Os), and weight if fluid status concerns
• Magnesium, phosphate 3 times per week
Weight, if fluid issues not of concern
Zinc, copper, folate, B-12: every 2-4 weeks, depending on baseline
• Tube feeding tolerance: nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, constipation
• Liver function tests, INR
• Clinical condition: temperature, blood pressure, current drug therapy
• C-reactive protein 2-3/week until stable
• Evaluate if goals are being met and re-evaluate goals. Move to twice weekly as patient begins to stabilize
• Full blood count, MCV, until stable
• Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine: baseline, then daily
• Glucose: baseline, then 1-2 per day, more if needed
• Magnesium, phosphate: baseline, daily if risk of refeeding syndrome
• Baseline: Liver function tests, INR, calcium, albumin, C-reactive protein, zinc, copper, full blood count and MCV, folate, B-12, iron, ferritin
• Selenium, if risk of depletion. Further testing dependent on baseline
• Baseline bone densitometry upon starting home parenteral nutrition, then every 2 years
Integrity and proper positioning of tubing
Review daily throughout course of treatment
Monitor for infection or pressure at site of insertion
Once stable
Nutrient intake, fluid balance (I/O)
• Electrolytes 1-2/week
Weight, BMI, and current drug therapy
• Evaluate if goals are being met, reevaluate goals
• Glucose
• Iron, ferritin every 3-6 months
• Magnesium, phosphate, calcium, albumin, full blood count, MCV
• Manganese, if on home PN, every 3-6 months
• Liver function tests, INR
• 25-OH vitamin D if on long-term support
